title: Contemporary Theories: Elitist, Pluralist, Schumpeter

cards.b:
Classical theory asked citizens to rule. Twentieth-century scholars looked at real democracies and found something else. Most people did not take part. Parties, bosses and experts took the decisions.

So a new group of theorists lowered the target. They defined democracy by what actually happens: competition for power, not rule by all. This is the realist or empirical turn. It fits the behavioural revolution in political science after 1945.

This topic is in the syllabus under "contemporary theories". You must know three strands: elite theory, Schumpeter's competitive democracy and pluralism (Dahl). Examiners also expect the critics: Bachrach and Baratz, Pateman, Macpherson, and the radical participatory school.

The three schools disagree on how power is spread.

  • Elitists: in every society, a small minority rules. Democracy changes who is in the elite, not the fact of elite rule.
  • Pluralists: power is dispersed among many groups. No one group always wins.
  • Schumpeter: leaders compete for the people's vote, much as firms compete for customers.

Schumpeter sits between the two. He accepts elite rule but sees voting competition as the democratic part.

Gaetano Mosca, The Ruling Class (1896)

In every society, two classes appear: a ruling minority and a ruled majority. The minority wins because it is organised. The many cannot organise as easily.

Vilfredo Pareto, The Mind and Society (1916)

Elites rule, but they circulate. Old elites decay and new ones replace them. He described two elite types, lions (who rule by force) and foxes (who rule by cunning). Revolutions merely swap elites.

Robert Michels, Political Parties (1911)

Even democratic parties and trade unions become oligarchies. Large organisations need leaders, experts and officials. This is the iron law of oligarchy: organisation means oligarchy.

All three were wary of democracy and Marxism. They held that equal rule by all is a myth.

cards.h: C. Wright Mills and the power elite
cards.b:
Elite theory also has a left-wing version. C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite (1956), argued that America was run by a small circle that overlapped across three institutions: big corporations, the military and the executive branch of government. They shared backgrounds and met in the same circles.

Unlike Pareto, Mills used elite theory to criticise democracy. The public, he said, had become a passive "mass", while real decisions were made at the top.

Note the difference from Marx: for Mills, the elite is based on holding institutional posts, not only on owning capital. It is also a response to Dahl's pluralism.

cards.h: Schumpeter: democracy as a competitive method
cards.b:
Joseph Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), rejected the "classical doctrine" that there is a common good the people want. In his view, voters are ill-informed and easily swayed. They have no clear will.

"The democratic method is that institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote."
Schumpeter, 1942

The role of the people is not to decide issues but to choose and remove leaders. Democracy is a way of picking rulers, a bit like a market. Political parties are firms and votes are the currency.

This is the minimalist or procedural view. It is also called the equilibrium model by Macpherson.

Robert Dahl, in A Preface to Democratic Theory (1956) and Who Governs? (1961), studied New Haven, Connecticut. He found that different groups led on different issues. Power was dispersed, not held by one elite. Leaders needed to bargain with many groups.

Earlier, David Truman, The Governmental Process (1951), saw politics as interest-group competition.

Dahl then coined polyarchy (Polyarchy, 1971): rule by the many, the best real-world approximation of democracy. Its institutions, in his later list, are:

  • Elected officials.
  • Free, fair and frequent elections.
  • Freedom of expression.
  • Alternative sources of information.
  • Associational autonomy.
  • Inclusive citizenship.

This list is a handy test of whether a country is a democracy.

• Bias in the system: E.E. Schattschneider, The Semisovereign People (1960), said the pluralist chorus sings with an upper-class accent. Business and the wealthy organise more easily than the poor.
  • Hidden power: Bachrach and Baratz (1962) showed that elites can keep issues off the agenda, so no visible contest occurs. This is the second face of power (see lesson 0-6-0).
  • Business privilege: Charles Lindblom, Politics and Markets (1977), moved from pluralism. Governments depend on business investment, so business has a privileged position. Dahl too later accepted that corporations distort equality (Dilemmas of Pluralist Democracy, 1982).
  • Neo-pluralism accepts these points but still defends group competition.

cards.h: The participatory reply to the realists
cards.b:
The realists seemed to say apathy is healthy. Carole Pateman, Participation and Democratic Theory (1970), pushed back. The realists had misread the old theory. Writers like Rousseau and J.S. Mill valued participation for its effect on citizens.

She argued that people learn democracy by practising it, especially in workplaces. Low participation is a problem to fix, not a fact to accept.

C.B. Macpherson likewise said that elitist models fit a market society and shrink democracy.

Others, such as Peter Bachrach (The Theory of Democratic Elitism, 1967), argued that elite theory protects the status quo.

These critiques lead to the participatory and deliberative models of the next lessons.

cards.h: Elites, parties and groups in India
cards.b:
• Michels in India: critics point to dynastic politics and top-down control in many parties. Intra-party democracy is weak. The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law, 52nd Amendment, 1985) gives party leaders strong control over legislators.
  • Congress system: Rajni Kothari argued that after independence one dominant party worked as a system of bargaining among factions ("The Congress System in India", 1964). It resembled a pluralist arena inside one party.
  • Interest groups: business bodies (FICCI, CII), unions and farmers' groups lobby. The farmers' agitation of 2020-21 ended with the repeal of the three farm laws in November 2021, which shows how organised groups can force change.
  • Money and elite capture: in February 2024 the Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme (ADR v Union of India) as violating the voter's right to information.

"Elite theory of democracy is the denial of democracy." Discuss.
Examine Schumpeter's view of democracy as a method.
Critically evaluate the pluralist theory of democracy.
"Iron law of oligarchy": does it apply to Indian parties?

Structure: define the shift from classical to realist theory. Give the three schools with one thinker and one book each. Use Dahl's polyarchy as the pluralist core. Then the critics: Schattschneider, Bachrach and Baratz, Lindblom, Pateman. Finish with Indian cases such as dynastic parties, farm laws repeal and electoral bonds. A table comparing the three schools earns marks.

quiz.q: The iron law of oligarchy was formulated by…
quiz.w: Michels, Political Parties (1911): organisation leads to oligarchy.

o: Old elites are replaced by new ones
quiz.w: Elites decay and are replaced, so rule by a few continues.

quiz.q: The Power Elite (1956) argues America was run by…
quiz.w: C. Wright Mills named corporate, military and executive leaders.

quiz.q: In Schumpeter's view, the people's main role is to…
quiz.w: Democracy is a competitive method for choosing leaders.

quiz.q: Dahl's study of New Haven appeared in…
Which is NOT one of Dahl's polyarchy institutions?
quiz.w: Dahl's list has no requirement for public ownership.

quiz.q: The upper-class accent remark about the pluralist chorus is by…
Bachrach and Baratz criticised pluralists for ignoring…
o: Non-decision-making that keeps issues off the agenda
quiz.w: Their 1962 article on the second face of power.
She criticised the realists and defended participation.
